title: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

relationships.phenotype: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: In four patients with EP AChR deficiency but with no mutations in AChR subunits, we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations
checks.explanation: Rapsyn-related CMS is associated with endplate AChR deficiency.

checks.claim: CMS11 is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RAPSN gene, which encodes rapsyn.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous rapsyn mutations.

checks.claim: The RAPSN gene is located on chromosome 11p11.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn, a 43-kDa postsynaptic protein, plays an essential role in the clustering of AChR at the EP.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature; the abstract does not state it explicitly.

paragraphs.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is an autosomal recessive postsynaptic disorder of the neuromuscular junction. It results from a deficiency of acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the endplate, caused by loss of function of rapsyn, the protein that clusters and anchors AChR at the postsynaptic membrane. Fatigable weakness usually begins at birth or in infancy, with ptosis, hypotonia, and feeding and breathing difficulties. Episodic crises with respiratory insufficiency are often brought on by intercurrent infections. Some patients have arthrogryposis or other congenital joint contractures. Onset in adolescence or adulthood also occurs. Patients usually respond to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, and some also respond to 3,4-diaminopyridine.

checks.claim: CMS11 is an autosomal recessive postsynaptic disorder of the neuromuscular junction.
checks.evidence_quote: The postsynaptic CMSs identified to date stem from a deficiency or kinetic abnormality of the acetylcholine receptor (AChR).
checks.explanation: The abstract describes postsynaptic AChR deficiency caused by recessive rapsyn mutations.

checks.claim: CMS11 results from a deficiency of acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the endplate.
checks.evidence_quote: EP studies in each case show decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR, as well as impaired postsynaptic morphological development.
checks.explanation: Endplate AChR deficiency.

checks.claim: The AChR deficiency in CMS11 is caused by loss of function of rapsyn.
checks.evidence_quote: none of the mutations hinders rapsyn self-association but that all three diminish coclustering of AChR with rapsyn
checks.explanation: The abstract shows reduced clustering function; it does not use the term 'loss of function'.

checks.claim: Rapsyn is the protein that clusters and anchors AChR at the postsynaptic membrane.
checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn, a 43-kDa postsynaptic protein, plays an essential role in the clustering of AChR at the EP.
checks.explanation: Clustering is stated; anchoring is implied by its link to the subsynaptic cytoskeleton.

checks.claim: In CMS11, fatigable weakness usually begins at birth or in infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: Most patients present in the first year and a few in later life.
checks.explanation: Most patients present in the first year, which matches onset at birth or in infancy.

checks.claim: Early CMS11 presentation includes ptosis, hypotonia, and feeding and breathing difficulties.
checks.evidence_quote: At birth, he presented with a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue
checks.explanation: The abstract reports hypotonia and breathing difficulty. Ptosis and feeding difficulties are not mentioned.

checks.claim: Patients with CMS11 often have episodic crises with respiratory insufficiency brought on by intercurrent infections.
checks.evidence_quote: The former is frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises.
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions life-threatening crises but does not say they involve respiratory insufficiency or are brought on by infections.

checks.evidence_quote: The former is frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises.
checks.explanation: Arthrogryposis is stated for the early-onset phenotype.

checks.evidence_quote: The late-onset phenotype developed in adolescence or adulthood
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

checks.evidence_quote: Most patients respond well to AChE inhibitors

checks.evidence_quote: some derive additional benefit from 3,4-DAP

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) described patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency who did not have mutations in the AChR subunit genes. Symptoms began early in life and included ptosis and fatigable weakness. The patients responded to anticholinesterase medication.

paragraphs.text: Burke et al. (2003) described 2 clinical subgroups among patients with rapsyn mutations. In the early-onset group, symptoms began at birth or in infancy. These patients had hypotonia, ptosis, bulbar weakness, and respiratory crises triggered by infections, and some had arthrogryposis multiplex congenita. In the late-onset group, symptoms began in adolescence or adulthood and could resemble seronegative myasthenia gravis. In both groups, ophthalmoparesis was mild or absent.

checks.claim: Burke et al. (2003) described 2 clinical subgroups, early-onset and late-onset, among patients with rapsyn mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: Two distinct phenotypes were noted: early and late onset.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes early- and late-onset phenotypes in patients with rapsyn mutations.

checks.claim: In the early-onset group of rapsyn-mutation patients described by Burke et al. (2003), symptoms began at birth or in infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: Two distinct phenotypes were noted: early and late onset. The former is frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita
checks.explanation: The abstract names an early-onset group but does not specify onset at birth or in infancy.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) described Near Eastern Jewish patients with a myasthenic syndrome caused by a mutation in the RAPSN promoter. These patients had distinctive facial malformations, including a long face and prognathism with malocclusion. Their myasthenic symptoms included ptosis and bulbar weakness, with little or no involvement of the limbs.

checks.claim: Ohno et al. (2003) described Near Eastern Jewish patients with a myasthenic syndrome caused by a mutation in the RAPSN promoter.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients 2-8 are of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations, and harbor -38A-->G that changes another E-box at -40 to -35
checks.explanation: Oriental Jewish patients of Iraqi or Iranian origin carry a RAPSN promoter mutation.

checks.claim: The Near Eastern Jewish patients with a RAPSN promoter mutation described by Ohno et al. (2003) had distinctive facial malformations, including a long face.
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions only 'facial malformations' and does not describe a long face. That detail may be in the full text, which was not supplied.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention prognathism or malocclusion. Only the abstract was supplied.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention ptosis. Only the abstract was supplied.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention bulbar weakness. Only the abstract was supplied.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not describe limb involvement. Only the abstract was supplied.

paragraphs.text: CMS11 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Affected individuals carry homozygous or compound heterozygous RAPSN mutations, and their heterozygous parents are unaffected (Ohno et al., 2002).

checks.claim: CMS11 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
checks.evidence_quote: we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations
checks.explanation: Recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Individuals affected with CMS11 carry homozygous or compound heterozygous RAPSN mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous.

checks.claim: Heterozygous parents of individuals with CMS11 are unaffected.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not discuss the parents.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) identified mutations in the RAPSN gene in patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency. All of these patients carried the asn88-to-lys (N88K) mutation, either in the homozygous state or in compound heterozygosity with a second RAPSN mutation. In expression studies, the mutant rapsyn was less able to cluster AChR.

checks.claim: Ohno et al. (2002) identified mutations in the RAPSN gene in patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: In four patients with EP AChR deficiency but with no mutations in AChR subunits, we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: All of the CMS patients studied by Ohno et al. (2002) carried the RAPSN asn88-to-lys (N88K) mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: All four patients carry N88K.

checks.claim: In the patients of Ohno et al. (2002), RAPSN N88K was present either in the homozygous state or in compound heterozygosity with a second RAPSN mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Homozygous or compound heterozygous.

checks.claim: In expression studies by Ohno et al. (2002), mutant rapsyn was less able to cluster AChR.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression studies in HEK cells indicate that none of the mutations hinders rapsyn self-association but that all three diminish coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.
checks.explanation: Reduced AChR clustering.

paragraphs.text: Richard et al. (2003) and Muller et al. (2003) found that the N88K mutation was frequent among patients with CMS of European origin. Haplotype analysis indicated that N88K is an ancient founder mutation in Indo-European populations. Muller et al. (2003) also identified other RAPSN mutations.

checks.claim: Richard et al. (2003) and Muller et al. (2003) found that the RAPSN N88K mutation was frequent among patients with CMS of European origin.
checks.explanation: The title does not state how frequent N88K is among European patients. Only the title was supplied.

checks.claim: Haplotype analysis indicated that RAPSN N88K is an ancient founder mutation in Indo-European populations.
checks.evidence_quote: The congenital myasthenic syndrome mutation RAPSN N88K derives from an ancient Indo-European founder.
checks.explanation: The title supports an ancient Indo-European founder origin. Haplotype analysis as the method is not stated in the title, the only text supplied.

checks.claim: Muller et al. (2003) identified RAPSN mutations other than N88K.
checks.explanation: The title mentions no RAPSN mutations other than N88K. Only the title was supplied.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a homozygous -38A-G mutation in Near Eastern Jewish patients with CMS and facial malformations. The mutation lies in an E-box element of the RAPSN promoter, and it impaired E-box-dependent transcriptional activation of RAPSN.

checks.claim: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a homozygous RAPSN -38A-G mutation in Near Eastern Jewish patients with CMS and facial malformations.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients 2-8 are of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations, and harbor -38A-->G
checks.explanation: The patients, their origin and the mutation all match. The abstract does not say the mutation is homozygous.

checks.claim: The RAPSN -38A-G mutation lies in an E-box element of the RAPSN promoter.
checks.evidence_quote: harbor -38A-->G that changes another E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG, which does not affect the consensus CANNTG sequence
checks.explanation: The mutation lies within an E-box of the RAPSN promoter.

checks.claim: The RAPSN -38A-G mutation impaired E-box-dependent transcriptional activation of RAPSN.
checks.evidence_quote: Luciferase reporter assays show that both -38A-->G and -27C-->G attenuate reporter gene expression in C2C12 myotubes, and that -27C-->G additionally attenuates reporter gene expression in MyoD- or myogenin-transfected HEK cells.
checks.explanation: -38A-G attenuates reporter expression, but it keeps the consensus E-box and gains binding. The MyoD/myogenin-dependent attenuation is shown only for -27C-G, so 'E-box-dependent activation' is an overstatement.

paragraphs.text: Burke et al. (2003) found that patients homozygous for N88K could have either the early-onset or the late-onset form of the disease. They therefore concluded that RAPSN genotype does not reliably predict disease severity.

checks.claim: Burke et al. (2003) found that patients homozygous for RAPSN N88K could have either the early-onset or the late-onset form of the disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract says only that N88K was common to all patients. It does not state that any patients were homozygous or relate N88K homozygosity to either phenotype.

checks.claim: Burke et al. (2003) concluded that RAPSN genotype does not reliably predict disease severity.
checks.explanation: The abstract contains no conclusion about whether genotype predicts severity.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) identified an asn88-to-lys (N88K) mutation in RAPSN in all of their patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency. The mutation was present either in the homozygous state or in compound heterozygosity with another RAPSN mutation. In expression studies, the mutant rapsyn was less able to cluster AChR.

checks.claim: Ohno et al. (2002) identified a RAPSN asn88-to-lys (N88K) mutation in all of their patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: N88K is present in all four patients.

checks.claim: In the patients of Ohno et al. (2002), RAPSN N88K was present either in the homozygous state or in compound heterozygosity with another RAPSN mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Homozygous or compound heterozygous.

checks.claim: In expression studies by Ohno et al. (2002), rapsyn carrying N88K was less able to cluster AChR.
checks.evidence_quote: none of the mutations hinders rapsyn self-association but that all three diminish coclustering of AChR with rapsyn
checks.explanation: All three mutations, including N88K, reduce coclustering.

paragraphs.text: Richard et al. (2003) and Muller et al. (2003) reported that N88K was the most common RAPSN mutation in patients of European origin. Haplotype analysis supported a single ancient founder event.

checks.explanation: The title does not say N88K is the most common mutation in European patients. Only the title was supplied.

checks.claim: Haplotype analysis supported a single ancient founder event for RAPSN N88K.
checks.evidence_quote: The congenital myasthenic syndrome mutation RAPSN N88K derives from an ancient Indo-European founder.
checks.explanation: The title supports a single ancient founder origin. That haplotype analysis supported it is not stated in the title, the only text supplied.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a homozygous -38A-G mutation in an E-box element of the RAPSN promoter in Near Eastern Jewish patients with CMS and facial malformations. The mutation impaired E-box-dependent transcription of RAPSN.

checks.claim: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a homozygous -38A-G mutation in an E-box element of the RAPSN promoter in Near Eastern Jewish patients with CMS and facial malformations.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients 2-8 are of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations, and harbor -38A-->G that changes another E-box at -40 to -35
checks.explanation: The E-box location, ethnicity and facial malformations match. The abstract does not state that the mutation is homozygous.

checks.claim: The RAPSN promoter -38A-G mutation impaired E-box-dependent transcription of RAPSN.
checks.evidence_quote: Luciferase reporter assays show that both -38A-->G and -27C-->G attenuate reporter gene expression in C2C12 myotubes
checks.explanation: The abstract shows reduced transcription, but it does not show the reduction is E-box-dependent for -38A-G. That variant preserves the consensus E-box, and the MyoD/myogenin effect was shown only for -27C-G.
